How Fluorescent Pins Work

Each end of an F4T5 bulb has two pins. Inside the glass, these two pins are connected by a tiny filament (like a toaster wire).

  1. To Start: The ballast sends electricity through the filament (in one pin, out the other) to heat it up. This "boils" off electrons into the gas.
  2. To Run: Once the gas is ionized, the electricity jumps across the long gap of the tube from one end to the other.

The Correct Way to Wire the Ends

Since your SC120-213-LT5 is an electronic ballast, it usually treats each end of the bulb as a single connection point. Here is how you should wire it:

Bulb LocationWiring Connection

End 2 (Right side)Connect both pins together and attach them to one Yellow wire.

On modern electronic "Rapid Start" or "Instant Start" ballasts like yours, it is standard practice to bridge (shunt) the two pins on each end together. This tells the ballast to just jump the arc across the tube immediately.

Crucial Warning:

turns.prompt_text: so when the ballast outputs electricity to the fluorescent bulbs what voltage does it use and what voltage does it spiked with
turns.response_html:
Since you’re coming at this from the perspective of a software engineer who’s worked with PCBs and electronics like the Raspberry Pi, you can think of a fluorescent ballast as a constant-current switching power supply with a very high-voltage startup phase.

Unlike a standard power supply that provides a steady 5V or 12V, a ballast’s voltage is dynamic.

1. The "Strike" Voltage (The Spike)

To get the light to turn on, the ballast has to overcome the resistance of the argon/mercury gas inside the tube. It does this by creating a massive potential difference.

  • Voltage: 600V to 1,000V+ AC.
  • What happens: This "spike" is a high-frequency burst (typically 20–60 kHz). It creates an "arc" through the gas.
  • Duration: This lasts only a fraction of a second—just long enough for the gas to ionize and become a conductor.

2. The "Running" Voltage (The Operating State)

Once the arc is established, the gas becomes a very low-resistance path. If the ballast kept pumping 1,000V, the bulb would explode.

  • Voltage: 50V to 100V AC (for small F4T5 bulbs, it’s often on the lower end, around 40V–60V).
  • What happens: The ballast "throttles" the voltage down to maintain a specific current (milliamps). This is why it’s called a ballast—it acts as a load-balancer to prevent the bulb from drawing too much power and destroying itself.

The Waveform Difference

In your PCB projects, you usually deal with DC. A fluorescent ballast is almost always High-Frequency AC.

  1. High Frequency (20kHz - 60kHz): Modern electronic ballasts like your "SugarCube" run at high frequencies. This is why they don't flicker like old-school 60Hz shop lights and why they don't "hum."
  2. Safety Note: Because the ballast uses high frequency and high voltage, don't use standard thin breadboard jumper wires for the bulb connections. Use wire rated for at least 600V (standard 18AWG or 22AWG hookup wire is usually fine) to ensure the insulation doesn't break down during the "strike" phase.

A Quick Warning for your DIY Setup

If you have the ballast powered on and the bulb isn't connected, the ballast will keep trying to "strike" (sending that 600V+ pulse) to find a lamp. This can eventually burn out the internal components of the ballast.

  • Always turn off the power before swapping bulbs or adjusting your 3D-printed fixture.

If that "strike" voltage from the ballast hits something other than the intended fluorescent tube, here is what happens:

1. The "Arc-Over" (Dielectric Breakdown)

Standard hookup wire or 3D-printed plastic has a "dielectric strength"—the maximum voltage it can block.

  • Breadboards & Jumpers: If you try to run this through a standard breadboard or thin jumper wires (usually rated for 30V–300V), the voltage will simply punch through the insulation.
  • The Result: You’ll see a blue spark (an arc) jumping between wires or from a wire to a nearby metal surface. This arc creates plasma, which is extremely hot and will melt your connectors or char your 3D-printed housing.

2. Destruction of Microcontrollers (ESP32 / Pi Pico)

If you are trying to "sense" the light or control it and that 1,000V spike leaks into your low-voltage rail:

  • Instant Death: CMOS chips (like the ones in your Raspberry Pi or Mac Mini) are rated for tiny voltages. A 1,000V spike will literally vaporize the microscopic traces inside the silicon.
  • The "Magic Smoke": Because ballasts operate at high frequencies (20–60kHz), this voltage can even "couple" capacitively into nearby wires that aren't even touching, causing interference or reboots in your other electronics.

3. Human Safety (The "Bite")

Because this is high-frequency AC, it behaves differently than the 60Hz from your wall outlet.

  • The "Skin Effect": High-frequency electricity tends to travel on the surface of conductors (including human skin).
  • The Sensation: While a ballast usually doesn't have enough current (amperage) to be immediately lethal like a microwave transformer, a 1,000V strike will cause a nasty, deep "RF burn" and a very painful shock that can throw your arm back.

How to Stay Safe in Your DIY Build

Since you’re likely designing a housing on your Bambu A1, follow these "Pro" rules for high-voltage projects:

  • Air Gaps: Keep your high-voltage wires (Red/Blue/Yellow) at least 10-15mm away from any low-voltage logic wires.
  • Wire Choice: Use wire labeled UL1015 or UL1007 (rated for 600V or 300V minimum). Even though 300V is below 1,000V, the insulation is usually thick enough for the split-second "strike" pulse.
  • Material: If you're printing the sockets, PETG is slightly better than PLA because it handles the heat from the bulb ends better and has decent insulating properties.

It is fascinating, isn't it? In electronics, we often focus on the "Big Three" ($Voltage$, $Current$, and $Resistance$), but once you move into AC systems like your ballast, Frequency (measured in Hertz) becomes the "invisible hand" that changes how electricity behaves.

The reason the frequency (Hz) matters so much for your safety and the bulb's performance comes down to two main concepts: The Skin Effect and Nervous System Interference.

1. The Nervous System and 60Hz

The human heart and nervous system operate using low-frequency electrical impulses.

  • The Danger Zone: Standard wall power (60Hz) is particularly dangerous because that frequency is close to the range that can interfere with the "timing" of your heart (causing ventricular fibrillation).
  • The Ballast Difference: Your Full House Cube operates at 20,000 to 60,000Hz (20–60kHz). At this high speed, your nerves literally cannot react fast enough to "feel" the individual cycles. Instead of a violent, bone-rattling shake, a high-frequency shock often feels like a sharp, intense heat or a "buzzing" sting.

2. The Skin Effect

As frequency increases, electricity tends to stop flowing through the center of a conductor and starts flowing only on the outer surface.

  • At 60Hz: The electricity flows through your entire arm, including deep tissue and organs.
  • At 40kHz: The electricity stays primarily on the surface of your skin. This is why a "hit" from a high-frequency ballast is more likely to cause a localized RF burn (Radio Frequency burn) on your finger rather than stopping your heart.

3. Why the Ballast Uses High Frequency

The ballast doesn't just use high frequency to be "safer"; it does it for efficiency, which is something you'll appreciate as a maker:

  • Smaller Components: High frequency allows the use of much smaller transformers and capacitors. That’s why your ballast is a tiny "SugarCube" instead of a heavy 10-pound iron brick like the ones from the 1970s.
  • Luminous Efficacy: Fluorescent gas actually glows more efficiently when excited at high frequencies. The phosphorus stays "excited" more consistently, which eliminates the visible flicker and the "hum" you find in older shop lights.

4. Impact on your DIY Projects

Because you're building an EEG headset, frequency is your biggest enemy.

  • EMI (Electromagnetic Interference): A ballast running at 40kHz is essentially a high-powered radio transmitter. If your EEG wires aren't shielded, they will act as antennas and pick up that 40kHz signal as massive "noise," completely drowning out the tiny brainwave signals (which are usually in the 0.5Hz–40Hz range).

turns.prompt_text: why do we still use fluorescent bulbs
turns.response_html:
It’s a great question, especially since LEDs have taken over about 90% of the market. While we are slowly phasing them out, there are several "maker" and industrial reasons why we haven't completely pulled the plug on fluorescent tech like your F4T5 setup.

1. UV and Specialized Light Spectrums

This is the biggest reason fluorescents still exist.

  • The LED Gap: LEDs are great at visible light, but they are relatively inefficient at producing high-intensity Ultraviolet (UV) light.
  • The Phosphor Advantage: In a fluorescent tube, the gas inside produces UV light naturally; the white coating (phosphor) on the glass just converts it to visible light. If you remove the phosphor, you have a perfect UV source.
  • Use Cases: We still use them for UV curing (perfect for your 3D resin prints), tanning beds, blacklights, and germicidal (UVC) lamps for sanitizing air and water.

2. 360-Degree Light Throw

LEDs are "directional"—they are tiny flat chips that blast light in one direction (usually 120°).

  • The Tube Advantage: A fluorescent tube is a "line source" that throws light in a perfect 360-degree cylinder.
  • Uniformity: In old-school office buildings or "back-lit" signs, fluorescents provide a very even, shadow-free glow that is hard to replicate with LEDs without using expensive diffusers that eat up some of the brightness.

3. Thermal Management

Since you’re a software engineer who tinkers with hardware, you know that heat is the enemy of semiconductors.

  • LEDs: They don't like heat. If you put a high-powered LED in a hot attic or near a furnace, the chip will degrade and dim quickly.
  • Fluorescents: They are "gas-state" electronics. They actually need a bit of heat to vaporize the mercury and work efficiently. They can survive in environments that would "cook" the driver of a cheap LED bulb.

4. "If It Ain't Broke" (Legacy Infrastructure)

There are billions of fluorescent ballasts (like your Full House Cube) already installed in the world.

  • Cost of Change: For a large warehouse with 5,000 fixtures, switching to LED often requires "re-wiring" to bypass the ballast (since many LEDs don't use them).
  • Maintenance: In some industrial settings, it's still cheaper to just swap a $3 tube than to hire an electrician to retro-fit a whole floor to LED.

The "Nostalgia" factor for Makers

For someone like you, who enjoys the "how it works" aspect of electronics:

  • The Start-up: There’s something tactile and satisfying about the flicker and "strike" of a fluorescent tube that an instant-on LED lacks.
  • Hackability: As you’re finding out, playing with 1,000V arcs and high-frequency gas discharge is a lot more "visceral" than just plugging in a 5V LED strip.

It is a massive scale when you stop to look up. In a store the size of a typical Fareway or a large supermarket, you’re looking at a massive electrical grid hidden in the ceiling.

There are a few "insider" reasons why grocery stores, in particular, have been the last holdouts for those long rows of fluorescent tubes:

1. The "Shadowless" Effect

Grocery stores are designed with High Vertical Illuminance. Because the shelves are tall and the aisles are narrow, they need light that wraps around the products.

  • LEDs can be "pointy," creating harsh shadows that make it hard to read labels on the bottom shelf.
  • Fluorescents are "line sources." The light emits from every inch of that 4-foot or 8-foot tube, filling the aisle from multiple angles so you don't cast a shadow on the cereal box you’re reaching for.

turns.prompt_text: what does shunted mean
turns.response_html:
In the context of fluorescent lighting and your Full House ballast, shunted refers to how the electrical current flows through the pins of the bulb socket (the "tombstone").

Since you're a software engineer, you can think of a shunted socket as having a hard-wired bridge (a short circuit) between the two contact points, whereas a non-shunted socket treats them as two independent "pins" on a bus.

The Technical Difference

  • Shunted Sockets: The two internal contacts are physically joined together. Electricity enters the socket and is instantly split between both pins of the bulb.
  • Non-Shunted Sockets: The two internal contacts are kept separate. They have two distinct wire "entry" points on the back of the socket. This allows the ballast to send a specific current through the bulb's internal filament to heat it up before striking the arc.

Which one do you need?

For your SC120-213-LT5 electronic ballast and F4T5 bulbs, the choice depends on the wiring style:

  1. Instant Start Ballasts: These almost always use shunted sockets. They don't care about heating the filament; they just blast the high voltage ($600V-1000V$) to strike the arc immediately.
  2. Rapid/Programmed Start Ballasts: These usually require non-shunted sockets because they need to pass a low-voltage "pre-heat" current through the filament first.

Recommended G5 (T5) Sockets

Since you are looking for connectors, here are the industry-standard options for your T5 setup:

  • For Versatility: The Leviton G5 Base Lampholder is a non-shunted socket. This is the "safe" buy because you can always turn a non-shunted socket into a shunted one by just jumping the wires together, but you can't do the reverse.

  • For Secure Mounting: If you're 3D printing a fixture on your Bambu A1, the Sunlite T5 Rotary Lock Socket is excellent. It uses a "turn-to-lock" mechanism that ensures the pins make solid contact, which is vital for preventing the high-voltage arcing we discussed.
